implementation_notes: C has no access control, so a god object is often not even a struct: it is a translation unit that declares a hundred `extern` globals and a few dozen `do_*` functions, with every other .c file including the same header. The absence of `static` is what makes it global, and the absence of an opaque handle is what makes it god-like. Detect with the compile database rather than by reading: how many translation units declare an `extern` variable defined in this one, and how many `do_` functions touch fields nobody else uses. Splitting means introducing an opaque struct (declare the type in a header, define it in exactly one .c file) and passing a pointer to it, which is the only encapsulation C offers.
idiom_name: one translation unit of extern globals plus do_* functions
pitfalls: `static` at file scope fixes accidental linkage but not god-ness: a file-private god object is still a god object, just invisible across translation units.
Because nothing is enforced, the 'split' can be undone by anyone adding one more `extern`; a header lint is the only guard.
`extern "C"` headers included from C++ propagate the whole global surface into the C++ side unchanged.
